name: Late Modernism
description: The continuation and transformation of high modernism after 1945 by writers formed by it, in Britain, Ireland and the United States: Samuel Beckett's prose trilogy and plays, Malcolm Lowry's Under the Volcano (1947), David Jones's The Anathemata (1952), William Carlos Williams's Paterson (1946-58), the late Cantos of Ezra Pound, Louis Zukofsky's "A" and Basil Bunting's Briggflatts (1966).
historical_context: By 1945 the founding modernists were dead or ageing, the war had discredited the mythic and totalising ambitions of the 1920s, and a new academic establishment was canonising modernism even as younger writers reacted against it.
aesthetic_principles: Difficulty, allusion and the autonomy of the work are kept but turned towards exhaustion, silence and the residue of the self; the long poem and the fragmented or reduced novel are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Either radical reduction (Beckett) or encyclopaedic accumulation (Pound, Zukofsky, Jones); narrators who doubt their own telling; history experienced as ruin.
historical_significance: It bridges high modernism and postmodernism: Beckett and the Objectivists are claimed by both. Critics such as Tyrus Miller (Late Modernism, 1999) use the term for modernism's own late phase, distinct from the postmodern break of the 1960s.

name: Existentialism in Anglophone Writing
description: The reception of French existentialism (Sartre, Camus, de Beauvoir) in British and American writing: Iris Murdoch's Sartre: Romantic Rationalist (1953) and Under the Net (1954), Colin Wilson's The Outsider (1956), Richard Wright's The Outsider (1953), Norman Mailer's essay "The White Negro" (1957) and Walker Percy's The Moviegoer (1961).
historical_context: Translations of Sartre and Camus reached English readers in the late 1940s; the war, the camps and the bomb made questions of freedom, absurdity and authentic choice urgent, and Beckett's and Ionesco's theatre gave them dramatic form.
aesthetic_principles: Fiction and essay organised around a solitary consciousness confronting a meaningless or hostile world; the philosophical novel, the confessional essay and the novel of ideas are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: The outsider or alienated hero; anguish, bad faith and the demand for authentic action; urban rootlessness; suspicion of systems and of bourgeois comfort.
historical_significance: It supplied the vocabulary of the 1950s outsider that the Angry Young Men, the Beats and the Theatre of the Absurd shared, and it gave way in the 1960s to structuralism, which displaced the existential subject.

name: The Angry Young Men
description: A journalistic label for British writers of the mid-1950s, mostly from lower-middle-class or provincial backgrounds, who attacked the establishment and class privilege: John Wain (Hurry On Down, 1953), Kingsley Amis (Lucky Jim, 1954), John Osborne (Look Back in Anger, 1956), Colin Wilson (The Outsider, 1956), John Braine (Room at the Top, 1957) and Alan Sillitoe (Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, 1958); Tom Maschler's anthology Declaration (1957) gathered them.
historical_context: Post-war austerity, the Butler Education Act of 1944 and the expansion of grammar-school and university places produced a generation educated beyond its parents' class; the Suez crisis of 1956 sharpened disillusion with Britain's rulers.
aesthetic_principles: Plain realist prose and naturalistic drama; the comic or furious first-person voice of a provincial hero; the novel and the play are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Hostility to snobbery, the Church and the BBC establishment; sexual frankness; the scholarship boy or working man on the make; comic deflation of pretension.
historical_significance: The label, popularised after the Royal Court publicised Osborne, was disowned by most of the writers, but the group ended the dominance of the Bloomsbury and country-house manner and opened the way for kitchen-sink drama and working-class fiction.

name: Working-Class and Regional Social Realism
description: Fiction and drama of industrial, provincial and working-class life written from inside it, chiefly in the North of England, Scotland and Wales, with an American counterpart: Alan Sillitoe, Stan Barstow (A Kind of Loving, 1960), David Storey (This Sporting Life, 1960), Keith Waterhouse (Billy Liar, 1959), Sid Chaplin, Barry Hines (A Kestrel for a Knave, 1968), Pat Barker (Union Street, 1982) and James Kelman; in the United States Harriette Arnow (The Dollmaker, 1954), Tillie Olsen (Tell Me a Riddle, 1961), Hubert Selby Jr. (Last Exit to Brooklyn, 1964) and Dorothy Allison (Bastard Out of Carolina, 1992).
historical_context: The persistence of class division through the welfare-state settlement, deindustrialisation from the 1970s and the miners' strike of 1984-85 gave the tradition its subjects; adult education and regional publishing gave it outlets.
aesthetic_principles: Documentary specificity of work, wages, housing and speech; dialect and vernacular narration; the realist novel, the short story and the stage or television play are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Factory, pit and estate settings; family and community under economic pressure; the conflict between solidarity and escape; vernacular voice treated as literary language.
historical_significance: It extends the Angry Young Men's realism beyond the 1950s and links the industrial novel of the nineteenth century with the Glasgow writers and the dirty realism of the 1980s.

name: Black Humour and the Absurdist Novel
description: Mainly American fiction that treats violence, war, death and institutional madness as farce: Joseph Heller's Catch-22 (1961), Kurt Vonnegut's Cat's Cradle (1963) and Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), Terry Southern's The Magic Christian (1959), J. P. Donleavy's The Ginger Man (1955), Thomas Pynchon's V. (1963) and John Barth's The Sot-Weed Factor (1960); Bruce Jay Friedman's anthology Black Humor (1965) named the tendency.
historical_context: The Cold War, nuclear deterrence, McCarthyism and Vietnam made official rationality look insane; the absurdist philosophy and theatre of the 1950s offered a vocabulary for it.
aesthetic_principles: Episodic plots, grotesque comedy and deadpan narration; the satirical novel and the picaresque are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Bureaucratic and military logic shown as lunatic; laughter at atrocity; flat characters in a manic world; apocalyptic endings.
historical_significance: It joins the absurdism of the 1950s to the postmodern fiction of the late 1960s and 1970s, into which most of its writers moved.

name: Postmodernism and Postmodern Fiction
description: The dominant international tendency in fiction from the 1960s, strongest in the United States and Britain: Thomas Pynchon (Gravity's Rainbow, 1973), John Barth, Donald Barthelme, Robert Coover, William Gaddis, Don DeLillo (White Noise, 1985), Kathy Acker, Ishmael Reed (Mumbo Jumbo, 1972), Paul Auster (The New York Trilogy, 1985-86), John Fowles (The French Lieutenant's Woman, 1969), Angela Carter, Salman Rushdie, Peter Ackroyd and Graham Swift.
historical_context: Consumer capitalism, mass media and the end of empire, together with structuralist and poststructuralist theory, undermined confidence in realist representation; Barth's "The Literature of Exhaustion" (1967) and theorists such as Ihab Hassan, Jean-François Lyotard (The Postmodern Condition, 1979; English 1984), Linda Hutcheon (A Poetics of Postmodernism, 1988) and Fredric Jameson (Postmodernism, 1991) defined it.
aesthetic_principles: Self-reflexivity, pastiche, parody and the mixing of high and popular forms; the encyclopaedic novel, historiographic metafiction and the short fiction collage are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Ontological uncertainty, paranoia and conspiracy, unreliable or plural narrators, collapsing boundaries between fiction and history, play with genre fiction.
historical_significance: It succeeds late modernism and incorporates black humour and metafiction; by the 1990s its techniques had been absorbed into mainstream and postcolonial fiction, and critics began to describe what came after it.

name: Metafiction
description: Fiction that draws attention to its own status as fiction; William H. Gass named it in Fiction and the Figures of Life (1970) and Patricia Waugh's Metafiction (1984) theorised it. English-language examples include Vladimir Nabokov's Pale Fire (1962), Muriel Spark's The Comforters (1957), John Barth's Lost in the Funhouse (1968), Robert Coover's Pricksongs and Descants (1969), John Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman (1969), B. S. Johnson's Christie Malry's Own Double-Entry (1973), Julian Barnes's Flaubert's Parrot (1984) and A. S. Byatt's Possession (1990).
historical_context: Structuralist linguistics and the sense that the conventions of realism had been exhausted led writers to make the making of fiction their subject.
aesthetic_principles: Intrusive authors, frames within frames, alternative endings, parodies of genre and of scholarship; the novel and the short story are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: The fiction that knows it is fiction; readers addressed directly; invented documents and footnotes; the author as a character.
historical_significance: A core technique of postmodern fiction, it is distinguished by Hutcheon's historiographic metafiction of the 1980s, in which self-consciousness is turned on the writing of history.

name: Experimental Fiction and the Anti-Novel
description: Fiction that breaks with linear narrative, the bound book or conventional syntax: in Britain B. S. Johnson (The Unfortunates, 1969, issued as loose sections in a box), Christine Brooke-Rose (Out, 1964; Thru, 1975), Ann Quin (Berg, 1964), Alan Burns, Eva Figes, Rayner Heppenstall and Gabriel Josipovici; in the United States William Gaddis (The Recognitions, 1955), Raymond Federman (Double or Nothing, 1971), Ronald Sukenick, Walter Abish (Alphabetical Africa, 1974), Gilbert Sorrentino and Kathy Acker, published by the Fiction Collective (1974) and Dalkey Archive Press (1984).
historical_context: The French nouveau roman of Robbe-Grillet and Sarraute and the example of Joyce and Beckett encouraged writers to treat realism as a convention; small presses made non-commercial fiction possible.
aesthetic_principles: Typographic and structural experiment, collage, cut-up and constraint; the novel, the novella and the short fiction sequence are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Discontinuous form, aleatory or reader-assembled order, visual layout, foregrounded language, refusal of plot and character as given.
historical_significance: It overlaps with metafiction and postmodernism but is defined by form rather than theme; its British phase ended with the deaths of Johnson (1973) and Quin (1973), while American surfiction (Federman's term, 1975) continued into the 1980s.

name: Southern Gothic
description: Fiction and drama of the American South that uses the grotesque, violence and decay to examine a haunted regional society: Flannery O'Connor (Wise Blood, 1952; A Good Man Is Hard to Find, 1955), Carson McCullers, Truman Capote (Other Voices, Other Rooms, 1948), Tennessee Williams, the late William Faulkner, Cormac McCarthy (Child of God, 1973) and Harry Crews (A Feast of Snakes, 1976).
historical_context: The South's history of slavery, defeat, segregation and religious intensity, and its resistance to the civil rights movement, gave its writers a subject in which the past is not past.
aesthetic_principles: The grotesque as moral and religious revelation; decaying houses and towns; the short story, the novel and the stage play are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Freakish or damaged characters, sudden violence, fundamentalist religion, racial guilt, isolation and family secrets.
historical_significance: It continues the Southern Renaissance of Faulkner's generation; O'Connor's essay "Some Aspects of the Grotesque in Southern Fiction" (1960) is its best-known statement, and its methods pass into the contemporary Gothic.

name: Magical Realism in English
description: Fiction in which the marvellous is narrated as an ordinary part of a realistically rendered world, adopted in English after the translation of Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1970): Salman Rushdie (Midnight's Children, 1981), Angela Carter (Nights at the Circus, 1984), Toni Morrison (Song of Solomon, 1977), Louise Erdrich (Tracks, 1988), Jeanette Winterson (Sexing the Cherry, 1989), Ben Okri (The Famished Road, 1991) and Ana Castillo (So Far from God, 1993).
historical_context: The Latin American boom and its translation, together with postcolonial and minority writers' search for forms that could hold suppressed histories and non-Western beliefs, carried the mode into English.
aesthetic_principles: The supernatural presented without authorial surprise; folk belief and myth set against official history; the novel is the principal genre.
defining_characteristics: Matter-of-fact miracles, ghosts and transformations; multigenerational family history; national allegory; oral storytelling.
historical_significance: Franz Roh coined the term (1925) and Alejo Carpentier's lo real maravilloso (1949) shaped it; in English it became a major idiom of postcolonial fiction, though critics dispute its application to writers who draw on their own traditions rather than on Latin American models.

name: Minimalism and Dirty Realism
description: American short fiction of the late 1970s and 1980s written in pared-down prose about working- and lower-middle-class lives: Raymond Carver (Will You Please Be Quiet, Please?, 1976; What We Talk About When We Talk About Love, 1981), Ann Beattie, Bobbie Ann Mason (Shiloh and Other Stories, 1982), Amy Hempel, Mary Robison, Frederick Barthelme, Tobias Wolff, Jayne Anne Phillips and Richard Ford. Granta 8, "Dirty Realism: New Writing from America" (1983), edited by Bill Buford, named the second tendency.
historical_context: The creative-writing programmes, the editor Gordon Lish at Esquire and Knopf, and the economic stagnation of the 1970s and 1980s shaped a fiction of diminished expectations.
aesthetic_principles: Omission, understatement, flat declarative sentences and open endings; the short story is the principal genre.
defining_characteristics: Trailer parks, motels, bars and suburbs; failing marriages, drink and unemployment; brand names and television; characters who cannot say what they feel.
historical_significance: It reacted against the maximalist postmodernism of Pynchon and Barth (Barth's "A Few Words About Minimalism", 1986, discussed it) and fed into the realist revival of the 1990s; the extent of Lish's editing of Carver is still debated.

name: Contemporary Gothic
description: Fiction that revives Gothic conventions for modern settings and psychological, sexual and social fears: Shirley Jackson (The Haunting of Hill House, 1959), Angela Carter (The Bloody Chamber, 1979), Anne Rice (Interview with the Vampire, 1976), Stephen King ('Salem's Lot, 1975), Joyce Carol Oates (Bellefleur, 1980), Susan Hill (The Woman in Black, 1983), Iain Banks (The Wasp Factory, 1984) and the writers gathered by Patrick McGrath and Bradford Morrow in The New Gothic (1991).
historical_context: The horror boom in paperback publishing from the 1970s, feminist rereadings of the Gothic and fascination with transgression and the unconscious renewed the form.
aesthetic_principles: Haunted houses, doubles, monsters and the uncanny as figures for repression; the novel, the short story and the fairy-tale retelling are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Confined or decaying spaces, female peril and female agency, the monstrous body, family secrets, ambiguity between the psychological and the supernatural.
historical_significance: It runs parallel to the commercial horror genre but crosses into literary fiction, and it draws on Southern Gothic and the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Gothic novel.

name: New Journalism
description: American nonfiction that used the techniques of fiction (scene, dialogue, point of view, status detail) for reporting: Tom Wolfe (The Kandy-Kolored Tangerine-Flake Streamline Baby, 1965; The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test, 1968), Gay Talese ("Frank Sinatra Has a Cold", Esquire, 1966), Truman Capote (In Cold Blood, 1966), Norman Mailer (The Armies of the Night, 1968), Joan Didion (Slouching Towards Bethlehem, 1968), Hunter S. Thompson (Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, 1971-72) and Michael Herr (Dispatches, 1977). Wolfe and E. W. Johnson's anthology The New Journalism (1973) defined it.
historical_context: Magazines such as Esquire under Harold Hayes, New York under Clay Felker and Rolling Stone gave writers space and licence to cover the counterculture, the Vietnam War and celebrity.
aesthetic_principles: Immersion reporting rendered through scene-by-scene construction and the reporter's subjectivity; literary journalism, the nonfiction novel and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Participatory or gonzo narration, extravagant style, reconstructed dialogue, the reporter as character.
historical_significance: It challenged the objectivity of conventional journalism and the boundary between fiction and fact, and it shaped later creative nonfiction and long-form magazine writing.

name: Second-Wave Feminist Writing
description: Fiction, poetry, polemic and criticism produced by and for the women's liberation movement in Britain and North America: Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963), Doris Lessing's The Golden Notebook (1962), Kate Millett's Sexual Politics (1970), Germaine Greer's The Female Eunuch (1970), Shulamith Firestone's The Dialectic of Sex (1970), Adrienne Rich's Diving into the Wreck (1973) and Of Woman Born (1976), Erica Jong's Fear of Flying (1973), Marilyn French's The Women's Room (1977) and the poetry of Audre Lorde.
historical_context: The movement grew out of civil rights and New Left politics; consciousness-raising groups, Ms. and Spare Rib (both 1972), and feminist presses such as Virago (1973), The Women's Press (1978) and Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press (1980) created a readership and a publishing base.
aesthetic_principles: Women's experience, the body and sexuality made public and political; the novel of awakening, confessional and lyric poetry, the manifesto and the polemical essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: The personal as political; marriage, motherhood, housework and sexuality examined critically; rediscovery of earlier women writers; debates between liberal, radical, socialist and Black feminisms.
historical_significance: It inherits Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex (English translation 1953) and produced feminist literary criticism; women of colour such as the contributors to This Bridge Called My Back (1981) challenged its white middle-class assumptions.

name: Jewish American Fiction
description: The flowering of American fiction by Jewish writers after the Second World War, centred in New York and Chicago: Saul Bellow (The Adventures of Augie March, 1953; Herzog, 1964), Bernard Malamud (The Assistant, 1957), Philip Roth (Goodbye, Columbus, 1959; Portnoy's Complaint, 1969), Grace Paley (The Little Disturbances of Man, 1959), Cynthia Ozick, Chaim Potok (The Chosen, 1967), E. L. Doctorow and Isaac Bashevis Singer in translation from Yiddish.
historical_context: Immigrant children's entry into the universities and the professions, the shock of the Holocaust, and the New York intellectual milieu of Partisan Review and Commentary shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Comic and moral realism, the urban idiom and Yiddish-inflected English; the novel and the short story are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Assimilation and its costs, the schlemiel and the suffering moralist, family and generational conflict, the memory of the Holocaust, sexual comedy.
historical_significance: It made immigrant experience central to American literature and opened the way for later ethnic literatures, while its writers often resisted the label.

name: Postwar African American Writing: Protest and Its Critics
description: The continuation of the Harlem Renaissance's legacy after 1945, divided between the protest tradition of Richard Wright and the writers who questioned it: Wright's The Outsider (1953), Ann Petry's The Street (1946), Ralph Ellison's Invisible Man (1952), James Baldwin's "Everybody's Protest Novel" (1949), Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953) and Notes of a Native Son (1955), Gwendolyn Brooks's Annie Allen (1949), Langston Hughes's Montage of a Dream Deferred (1951), Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun (1959) and Paule Marshall's Brown Girl, Brownstones (1959).
historical_context: The Great Migration, wartime service, the Cold War and the early civil rights movement (Brown v. Board of Education, 1954; the Montgomery bus boycott, 1955-56) framed the struggle over integration and identity.
aesthetic_principles: Realist and naturalist protest fiction alongside modernist experiment and the personal essay; the novel, the essay, lyric poetry and the stage play are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Racial injustice and urban segregation; invisibility and double consciousness; the critique of protest as a confining form; jazz and blues as models of art.
historical_significance: It links the Harlem Renaissance to the Black Arts Movement, which rejected its integrationist aims; Brooks's Pulitzer Prize (1950) and Hansberry's Broadway success marked new public recognition.

name: Black Arts Movement
description: The artistic arm of Black Power, launched when Amiri Baraka (LeRoi Jones) founded the Black Arts Repertory Theatre/School in Harlem after the assassination of Malcolm X in 1965: Baraka, Larry Neal ("The Black Arts Movement", 1968), Sonia Sanchez, Nikki Giovanni, Haki R. Madhubuti, Etheridge Knight (Poems from Prison, 1968), Jayne Cortez, Mari Evans, Ed Bullins and, after 1967, Gwendolyn Brooks. Baraka and Neal's anthology Black Fire (1968) and Addison Gayle's The Black Aesthetic (1971) are its key texts.
historical_context: Urban uprisings, Black nationalism and the shift from civil rights to Black Power; Broadside Press (Detroit, 1965), Third World Press (Chicago, 1967), Negro Digest/Black World and community theatres gave it institutions.
aesthetic_principles: Art for and by the Black community, judged by a Black aesthetic; performance-oriented free verse, ritual and agitprop drama, and the manifesto are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Black vernacular, jazz rhythm and oral performance; revolutionary nationalism; rejection of white Western standards; collective rather than individual voice.
historical_significance: It rejected the integrationist postwar tradition and shaped later spoken-word and hip-hop poetry; critics have discussed its sexism and homophobia, and its institutions declined after the mid-1970s.

name: Native American Renaissance
description: The surge of fiction and poetry by Native American writers that followed N. Scott Momaday's House Made of Dawn (1968; Pulitzer Prize 1969): James Welch (Winter in the Blood, 1974), Leslie Marmon Silko (Ceremony, 1977), Simon Ortiz, Gerald Vizenor, Paula Gunn Allen, Louise Erdrich (Love Medicine, 1984), Joy Harjo, Linda Hogan and Sherman Alexie; Kenneth Lincoln's Native American Renaissance (1983) named it.
historical_context: The Red Power movement, the occupation of Alcatraz (1969-71) and Vine Deloria Jr.'s Custer Died for Your Sins (1969) asserted sovereignty and cultural survival against termination and assimilation policies.
aesthetic_principles: Oral tradition, ceremony and tribal history woven into the modern novel and lyric; the novel, the short story cycle and lyric poetry are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Return and healing of a damaged protagonist; land and place as sacred; trickster figures; mixed-blood identity; non-linear, cyclical time.
historical_significance: It made Native writing a recognised part of American literature; later writers and critics have questioned the term for implying that nothing came before 1968.

name: Chicano Movement Literature
description: Mexican American literature produced in and after El Movimiento: Rodolfo "Corky" Gonzales's I Am Joaquín (1967), Luis Valdez's El Teatro Campesino (1965) and Zoot Suit (1978), Tomás Rivera's ...y no se lo tragó la tierra (1971), Rudolfo Anaya's Bless Me, Ultima (1972), Rolando Hinojosa, Alurista, Oscar Zeta Acosta, Lorna Dee Cervantes, Sandra Cisneros (The House on Mango Street, 1984) and Gloria Anzaldúa (Borderlands/La Frontera, 1987).
historical_context: The farmworkers' strikes led by César Chávez and Dolores Huerta, student walkouts and the idea of Aztlán as homeland; Quinto Sol Publications and Arte Público Press (1979) published the work.
aesthetic_principles: Bilingual and code-switching language, the corrido and oral storytelling; poetry, actos (short agitprop plays), the novel and the short story cycle are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Barrio and borderland life, migrant labour, indigenous and mestizo identity, Catholic and curandera traditions, the search for an ancestral homeland.
historical_significance: It established Chicano literature as a field; Chicana writers of the 1980s challenged its masculinism and opened it to feminist and queer perspectives.

name: Asian American Literary Movement
description: Writing that defined an Asian American literature and recovered earlier work: the anthology Aiiieeeee! (1974), edited by Frank Chin, Jeffery Paul Chan, Lawson Fusao Inada and Shawn Wong; Maxine Hong Kingston's The Woman Warrior (1976); Frank Chin's plays; the recovery of John Okada's No-No Boy (1957), Carlos Bulosan's America Is in the Heart (1946) and Louis Chu's Eat a Bowl of Tea (1961); and later Amy Tan, David Henry Hwang (M. Butterfly, 1988), Jessica Hagedorn, Bharati Mukherjee and Chang-rae Lee.
historical_context: The Asian American movement of the late 1960s, ethnic studies programmes (San Francisco State, 1968-69), the 1965 Immigration Act and the memory of Japanese American internment shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Recovery of history and voice against stereotype; the memoir, the novel, the play and lyric poetry are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Generational conflict, immigration and internment, the model-minority myth, talk-story and myth retold, debates over authenticity.
historical_significance: Its founding anthologists clashed publicly with Kingston and Tan over the use of Chinese myth (the Chin-Kingston debate), and by the 1990s the field had widened to South Asian, Filipino and Korean American writing.

name: Black British Writing and the Windrush Generation
description: Literature by Caribbean, African and Asian migrants to Britain and their children, beginning with the arrival of the Empire Windrush in 1948: Sam Selvon (The Lonely Londoners, 1956), George Lamming (The Emigrants, 1954), E. R. Braithwaite, Andrew Salkey, Buchi Emecheta (Second-Class Citizen, 1974), James Berry, Linton Kwesi Johnson, Grace Nichols, John Agard, Caryl Phillips, David Dabydeen, Hanif Kureishi (The Buddha of Suburbia, 1990), Jackie Kay, Meera Syal and Bernardine Evaristo.
historical_context: Post-war migration from the Commonwealth, racism and riots (Notting Hill, 1958; Brixton, 1981), the BBC's Caribbean Voices (1943-58) and presses such as New Beacon Books (1966) and Bogle-L'Ouverture (1968) shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: London and the provincial city seen by the newcomer; creole and nation language; the novel, poetry in performance and print, and drama are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Arrival and disillusion, racism and belonging, the second generation's divided identity, music and street speech, revisions of Englishness.
historical_significance: It overlaps with Caribbean and African literature in English and with dub and performance poetry, and by the 1990s it had moved from the margins to the centre of British fiction.

name: Caribbean Literature in English
description: The literature of the English-speaking Caribbean and its diaspora: Derek Walcott (Omeros, 1990), Kamau Brathwaite (The Arrivants, 1973), V. S. Naipaul (A House for Mr Biswas, 1961), Wilson Harris (Palace of the Peacock, 1960), George Lamming (In the Castle of My Skin, 1953), Sam Selvon, Roger Mais, Jean Rhys (Wide Sargasso Sea, 1966), Louise Bennett, Earl Lovelace, Merle Hodge, Erna Brodber, Jamaica Kincaid, Olive Senior and Lorna Goodison; the Caribbean Artists Movement (London, 1966-72) and the magazines Bim, Kyk-Over-Al and Savacou were its forums.
historical_context: Decolonisation and independence (Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago, 1962; Barbados and Guyana, 1966), emigration to Britain and North America, and debates about creole language and African heritage shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Creole and Standard English in tension, Brathwaite's nation language, the epic and the folk tale; the novel, lyric and epic poetry, and drama are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Exile and return, colonial education, plantation history, carnival and calypso, race and creolisation, the island as microcosm.
historical_significance: It produced two Nobel laureates (Walcott, 1992; Naipaul, 2001) and shaped postcolonial theory's ideas of hybridity and creolisation.

name: African Literature in English
description: Anglophone literature of West, East and Southern Africa from Amos Tutuola's The Palm-Wine Drinkard (1952): Cyprian Ekwensi, Chinua Achebe (Things Fall Apart, 1958), Wole Soyinka (Nobel Prize 1986), Christopher Okigbo, J. P. Clark, Gabriel Okara, Flora Nwapa, Buchi Emecheta, Ama Ata Aidoo, Ayi Kwei Armah, Kofi Awoonor, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Okot p'Bitek, Bessie Head, Nuruddin Farah, Dambudzo Marechera, Tsitsi Dangarembga and Ben Okri.
historical_context: Independence movements and the new nations (Ghana, 1957; Nigeria, 1960; Kenya, 1963), then civil war and dictatorship; the Mbari Club (Ibadan, 1961), Black Orpheus (1957), Transition (1961), the Makerere conference of 1962 and Heinemann's African Writers Series (1962) supplied its institutions.
aesthetic_principles: Oral tradition, proverb and myth adapted to the novel, lyric and drama; the language question (Ngũgĩ's turn to Gikuyu in the late 1970s); the novel, poetry and drama are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Colonial encounter and its aftermath, village and city, the disillusion of independence, women's lives under tradition and modernity, political violence.
historical_significance: It re-wrote the colonial image of Africa (Achebe's "An Image of Africa" answered Conrad) and became central to postcolonial studies.

name: South African Writing under Apartheid
description: English-language writing produced in and against the apartheid state from the National Party's victory in 1948 to the elections of 1994: Alan Paton (Cry, the Beloved Country, 1948), Peter Abrahams, the Drum writers (Can Themba, Bloke Modisane, Lewis Nkosi), Es'kia Mphahlele (Down Second Avenue, 1959), Alex La Guma, Nadine Gordimer, Athol Fugard, Dennis Brutus, Mongane Wally Serote, Miriam Tlali, Njabulo Ndebele and J. M. Coetzee.
historical_context: Censorship, banning orders, exile and the Sharpeville (1960) and Soweto (1976) massacres; Drum magazine in the 1950s and Staffrider (1978) gave Black writers outlets.
aesthetic_principles: Testimony and protest set against irony and allegory; the novel, the short story, protest poetry and workshop theatre are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Racial segregation and the pass laws, prison and exile, the liberal conscience under strain, township life, the writer's responsibility.
historical_significance: It produced two Nobel laureates (Gordimer, 1991; Coetzee, 2003), and Ndebele's call for a "rediscovery of the ordinary" (1984) marked the turn away from protest writing.

name: South Asian Literature in English
description: English-language writing from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh and their diasporas after independence and partition: R. K. Narayan, Mulk Raj Anand, Raja Rao, Nirad C. Chaudhuri, Kamala Markandaya, Ruth Prawer Jhabvala, Anita Desai, Nissim Ezekiel, A. K. Ramanujan, Kamala Das, Arun Kolatkar, Salman Rushdie (Midnight's Children, 1981), Bapsi Sidhwa, Amitav Ghosh, Vikram Seth (A Suitable Boy, 1993), Rohinton Mistry, Shyam Selvadurai and Arundhati Roy (The God of Small Things, 1997).
historical_context: Independence and partition in 1947, the debate over English as an Indian language, the Writers Workshop of Calcutta (P. Lal, 1958) and the international success of Midnight's Children shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Indian English idiom, myth and epic adapted to realist and magical-realist narrative; the novel, the short story and lyric poetry are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Partition and nationhood, family and caste, the city and the small town, exile and diaspora, language and translation.
historical_significance: Rushdie's Booker Prize (1981) inaugurated an international vogue; critics debate the privileging of English-language writing over the literatures of India's other languages.

name: Postcolonial Literature
description: An umbrella term, established by Bill Ashcroft, Gareth Griffiths and Helen Tiffin's The Empire Writes Back (1989), for writing in English from former colonies and their diasporas that answers colonialism and its aftermath; it gathers the Caribbean, African, South Asian, Australian, New Zealand and Canadian literatures and writers such as Achebe, Walcott, Naipaul, Rushdie, Ngugi, Soyinka, Coetzee and Ondaatje.
historical_context: Decolonisation from 1947 onwards, migration to the former imperial centres and the institutional growth of 'Commonwealth literature' studies (the Journal of Commonwealth Literature, 1965) shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Writing back to the canon, appropriation of English, hybrid forms drawing on oral and indigenous traditions; the novel, poetry and drama are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Rewritings of canonical texts (Wide Sargasso Sea, Foe), the politics of language, nation and history, exile and diaspora, hybridity.
historical_significance: It replaced 'Commonwealth literature' as the field's name in the late 1980s and is closely tied to postcolonial theory; critics have questioned whether one term can describe such different literatures.

name: Indigenous Writing in Australia, Canada and New Zealand
description: Writing in English by Aboriginal Australian, Māori and First Nations authors: in Australia Oodgeroo Noonuccal (We Are Going, 1964), Kevin Gilbert, Jack Davis (No Sugar, 1985), Sally Morgan (My Place, 1987) and Ruby Langford Ginibi; in New Zealand Hone Tuwhare (No Ordinary Sun, 1964), Witi Ihimaera (Pounamu, Pounamu, 1972), Patricia Grace (Potiki, 1986), Keri Hulme (The Bone People, 1984) and Alan Duff; in Canada Maria Campbell (Halfbreed, 1973), Lee Maracle, Jeannette Armstrong (Slash, 1985), Beatrice Culleton, Tomson Highway (The Rez Sisters, 1986) and Thomas King.
historical_context: Land-rights and civil-rights movements (the Australian referendum of 1967, the Māori Land March of 1975, the Canadian protests against the 1969 White Paper) and Indigenous presses and theatres made the writing possible.
aesthetic_principles: Oral story, song and kinship woven into English-language forms; life writing, the novel, poetry and drama are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Dispossession and stolen generations, land and spiritual connection, residential schools and missions, survival and cultural renewal.
historical_significance: It parallels the Native American Renaissance; identity controversies (for example over Mudrooroo in 1996) have shaped debates about Indigenous authorship.

name: Canadian Literary Nationalism
description: The emergence of a self-consciously national English-Canadian literature: Margaret Laurence (The Stone Angel, 1964), Alice Munro (Dance of the Happy Shades, 1968), Mordecai Richler, Robertson Davies (Fifth Business, 1970), Leonard Cohen, Al Purdy, Margaret Atwood (Survival, 1972), Dennis Lee, Rudy Wiebe, Timothy Findley, Marian Engel and Michael Ondaatje; Northrop Frye's "Conclusion" to the Literary History of Canada (1965) and its "garrison mentality" framed it.
historical_context: The Massey Report (1951), the Canada Council (1957), the centennial of 1967 and new presses such as Coach House (1965) and House of Anansi (1967) supported it against American cultural dominance.
aesthetic_principles: The search for a Canadian identity in landscape, survival and the small town; the novel, the short story and lyric poetry are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Wilderness and victimhood, regional and prairie life, the Ontario small town, ambivalence towards Britain and the United States.
historical_significance: It produced the 'CanLit' institutions of the 1970s; from the 1980s multicultural and Indigenous writers challenged its largely Anglo-Canadian definition of the nation.

name: Welsh Writing in English: The Second Flowering
description: The renewal of Anglo-Welsh writing from the 1960s, after the 'first flowering' of Dylan Thomas's generation: R. S. Thomas, Dannie Abse, Glyn Jones (The Dragon Has Two Tongues, 1968), Emyr Humphreys (Outside the House of Baal, 1965), Raymond Garlick, Roland Mathias, John Ormond, Leslie Norris, Harri Webb, Gillian Clarke, Tony Conran and Raymond Williams (Border Country, 1960); Meic Stephens founded Poetry Wales (1965).
historical_context: The language campaigns of the 1960s, the drowning of Tryweryn (1965) and the growth of Welsh nationalism led English-language writers to examine their relation to Welsh culture.
aesthetic_principles: Landscape, community and history rendered in a restrained lyric and realist manner; lyric poetry and the novel are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: The Welsh language and its loss, rural and industrial Wales, chapel and community, national identity.
historical_significance: It established Welsh writing in English as a field, supported by the Welsh Arts Council and The Anglo-Welsh Review (1957-88).

name: The Scottish Literary Revival of the 1980s and 1990s
description: A renewal of Scottish fiction, poetry and drama dated from Alasdair Gray's Lanark (1981): James Kelman (How Late It Was, How Late, Booker Prize 1994), Tom Leonard, Liz Lochhead, Agnes Owens, Jeff Torrington, Janice Galloway (The Trick Is to Keep Breathing, 1989), A. L. Kennedy, Iain Banks, Irvine Welsh (Trainspotting, 1993), Duncan McLean and Alan Warner; several began in Philip Hobsbaum's Glasgow writers' group of the early 1970s.
historical_context: The failed devolution referendum of 1979, Thatcherism and deindustrialisation turned writers to questions of Scottish identity, class and language; Polygon Books and small magazines published them.
aesthetic_principles: Glaswegian and Edinburgh vernacular as narrative language, formal experiment and fantasy alongside realism; the novel, the short story and poetry are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Working-class urban life, unemployment and addiction, typographic and narrative experiment, political allegory, women's inner lives.
historical_significance: It follows the earlier Scottish Renaissance of MacDiarmid's generation and is often linked to the cultural mood that led to devolution in 1997-99.

name: Northern Irish Poetry and the Belfast Group
description: Poetry from Northern Ireland that emerged around Philip Hobsbaum's Belfast Group (from 1963): Seamus Heaney (Death of a Naturalist, 1966; Nobel Prize 1995), Michael Longley, Derek Mahon, James Simmons, Paul Muldoon, Ciarán Carson (The Irish for No, 1987), Medbh McGuckian and Frank Ormsby (The Honest Ulsterman, 1968); the Field Day Theatre Company (1980) of Brian Friel and Stephen Rea extended the project to drama and criticism.
historical_context: The Troubles from 1968, the inheritance of Yeats and Kavanagh, and access to university education for Catholic as well as Protestant students shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Formal control, close attention to place and language, and oblique treatment of violence; lyric poetry is the principal genre, with verse drama and criticism through Field Day.
defining_characteristics: Rural childhood and the bog, sectarian violence, the poet's responsibility, language and naming, ironic and playful indirection (Muldoon).
historical_significance: It made Northern Ireland a centre of English-language poetry; debates about the poet's obligation to address the Troubles accompanied it throughout.

name: Gay and Lesbian Literature after Stonewall
description: Openly gay and lesbian writing that followed the Stonewall riots of 1969: Rita Mae Brown (Rubyfruit Jungle, 1973), Andrew Holleran (Dancer from the Dance, 1978), Larry Kramer, Armistead Maupin (Tales of the City, 1978), Edmund White (A Boy's Own Story, 1982) and the Violet Quill, Audre Lorde (Zami, 1982), Jeanette Winterson (Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit, 1985), Alan Hollinghurst (The Swimming-Pool Library, 1988), Paul Monette, Thom Gunn (The Man with Night Sweats, 1992) and Tony Kushner (Angels in America, 1991-93).
historical_context: Gay liberation and lesbian feminism, then the AIDS epidemic from 1981; Naiad Press (1973), the Gay Men's Press (1979) and the Lambda Literary Awards (1989) supported it.
aesthetic_principles: Coming-out narrative, urban gay life and testimony; the novel, memoir, lyric poetry and drama are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Coming out, community and desire, homophobia, AIDS and mourning, chosen family.
historical_significance: It built on pre-Stonewall works such as Gore Vidal's The City and the Pillar (1948), James Baldwin's Giovanni's Room (1956) and Christopher Isherwood's A Single Man (1964), and it fed into queer theory around 1990.

name: The Movement
description: A group of English poets and novelists of the 1950s who favoured rational, ironic, formally traditional writing: Philip Larkin, Kingsley Amis, Donald Davie, D. J. Enright, Elizabeth Jennings, Thom Gunn, John Holloway, John Wain and Robert Conquest. J. D. Scott named them in The Spectator ("In the Movement", 1 October 1954); Enright's Poets of the 1950s (1955) and Conquest's New Lines (1956) are its anthologies.
historical_context: Austerity Britain, the welfare state and the redbrick and Oxbridge-educated lower middle class; a reaction against the neo-Romanticism of Dylan Thomas and the apocalyptic poets of the 1940s.
aesthetic_principles: Clarity, irony, regular metre and rhyme, and the plain speaking voice; lyric poetry and the comic novel are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Empirical scepticism, suspicion of rhetoric and myth, provincial and domestic settings, understatement and wit.
historical_significance: It dominated English poetry in the 1950s; A. Alvarez's anthology The New Poetry (1962) attacked its 'gentility', and the Group, the Liverpool poets and the British Poetry Revival defined themselves against it.

name: The Group
description: A London workshop of poets convened by Philip Hobsbaum (from 1955) and later Edward Lucie-Smith, who met weekly to criticise poems circulated in advance: Peter Porter, Peter Redgrove, George MacBeth, Martin Bell, Alan Brownjohn, Edward Lucie-Smith and others; A Group Anthology (1963) collected their work.
historical_context: Hobsbaum brought the Cambridge habit of practical criticism to a writers' workshop; the BBC's Third Programme and small presses gave members an audience.
aesthetic_principles: Close critical reading applied to work in progress; the dramatic monologue and the lyric are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Directness, social and sexual frankness, satire, and an emphasis on poems that survive public criticism.
historical_significance: A short-lived but influential model of the poetry workshop, later repeated by Hobsbaum in Belfast (1963) and Glasgow (1971).

name: The British Poetry Revival
description: The modernist and international current in British poetry of the 1960s and 1970s, named by Eric Mottram's lecture "The British Poetry Revival 1960-1974": Basil Bunting's return with Briggflatts (1966), J. H. Prynne and the Cambridge poets, Roy Fisher, Tom Raworth, Lee Harwood, Gael Turnbull, Bob Cobbing, Allen Fisher, Barry MacSweeney and Tom Pickard, published by Fulcrum, Goliard, Trigram and Ferry presses and, from 1971 to 1977, in Poetry Review under Mottram.
historical_context: Contact with American Black Mountain, Objectivist and New York poetry, the Morden Tower readings in Newcastle (from 1964) and a small-press boom outside the London literary establishment.
aesthetic_principles: Open form, collage, sound and visual experiment, and the Poundian and Objectivist inheritance; lyric sequence, long poem and concrete or sound poem are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Difficulty and discontinuity, attention to place and the materials of language, hostility to the mainstream 'Movement' lyric.
historical_significance: Excluded from the major anthologies of the period, it was gathered later in A Various Art (1987) and The New British Poetry (1988) and continues in the 'linguistically innovative' poetry of the 1990s.

name: The Liverpool Poets and the British Underground
description: Popular, performance-centred poetry of the 1960s counterculture: Adrian Henri, Roger McGough and Brian Patten in The Mersey Sound (Penguin Modern Poets 10, 1967); the International Poetry Incarnation at the Royal Albert Hall (11 June 1965); Michael Horovitz's Children of Albion: Poetry of the Underground in Britain (1969); Pete Brown, Adrian Mitchell and Christopher Logue.
historical_context: The Liverpool beat-music scene, the Beat poets' visits to Britain and the youth culture of the 1960s took poetry into pubs, clubs and concert halls.
aesthetic_principles: Accessible, humorous and lyrical verse written for reading aloud; performance poetry and the popular lyric are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Pop-culture reference, urban romance, anti-war protest, comic surprise, jazz and rock accompaniment.
historical_significance: It brought mass audiences to poetry (The Mersey Sound became one of the best-selling poetry anthologies) and anticipated later performance and punk poetry.

name: Confessional Poetry
description: American poetry of intimate autobiographical disclosure: Robert Lowell's Life Studies (1959), W. D. Snodgrass's Heart's Needle (1959), Anne Sexton's To Bedlam and Part Way Back (1960), Sylvia Plath's Ariel (1965) and John Berryman's The Dream Songs (1964-68); M. L. Rosenthal used the term in reviewing Life Studies (1959). Lowell's Boston University seminar of 1958-59 brought Plath and Sexton together.
historical_context: Postwar psychotherapy, the private life of the suburban family and the cultural pressure on women and men to conform made breakdown, divorce and suicide poetic subjects.
aesthetic_principles: The first-person lyric as unmediated testimony, yet tightly crafted; lyric sequence and the dramatic lyric are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Mental illness and hospitalisation, family and marriage, sexuality, suicide and death, the self as subject.
historical_significance: It broke with the impersonal New Critical lyric and shaped the autobiographical mainstream of later poetry; the poets themselves often rejected the label.

name: The Beat Generation
description: A circle of American writers formed in New York in the mid-1940s and centred later in San Francisco: Allen Ginsberg (Howl and Other Poems, 1956), Jack Kerouac (On the Road, 1957), William S. Burroughs (Naked Lunch, 1959), Gregory Corso, Lawrence Ferlinghetti, Gary Snyder, Michael McClure, Diane di Prima, Bob Kaufman, Joyce Johnson and Herbert Huncke; John Clellon Holmes's Go (1952) and "This Is the Beat Generation" (1952) introduced them, and the Six Gallery reading (San Francisco, 7 October 1955) made them public.
historical_context: Postwar conformity and Cold War anxiety, bebop jazz, drugs, Buddhism and the road; the obscenity trials of Howl (1957) and Naked Lunch (1966) made them notorious.
aesthetic_principles: Spontaneous composition, the long breath-line and the oral performance; free verse, the autobiographical novel and the cut-up are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Visionary candour, sexual openness, spiritual quest, travel and rootlessness, jazz rhythm, opposition to materialism.
historical_significance: It anticipated the 1960s counterculture and overlapped with the San Francisco Renaissance and the Black Mountain and New York poets gathered in Donald Allen's The New American Poetry 1945-1960 (1960).

name: The San Francisco Renaissance
description: Poetry centred in the San Francisco Bay Area after the war: Kenneth Rexroth, Robert Duncan, Jack Spicer (After Lorca, 1957), William Everson (Brother Antoninus), Philip Lamantia, Madeline Gleason, Philip Whalen and Lawrence Ferlinghetti, whose City Lights bookshop (1953) and Pocket Poets series published the Beats.
historical_context: Pacifist and anarchist circles of the war years, the Berkeley poetry scene and the 1955 Six Gallery reading made San Francisco an alternative to New York; the Berkeley Poetry Conference (1965) closed the period.
aesthetic_principles: Poetry as spoken and communal, drawing on mysticism, myth and the West Coast landscape; lyric, serial poem and public reading are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Anarchist politics, occult and religious vision, the serial poem (Spicer), Asian influence, readings as events.
historical_significance: It overlaps with the Beats and Black Mountain and is one of the groups in Donald Allen's The New American Poetry (1960).

name: The New York School
description: Poets associated with New York painters and galleries in the 1950s and 1960s: Frank O'Hara (Meditations in an Emergency, 1957; Lunch Poems, 1964), John Ashbery (Some Trees, 1956; Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror, 1975), Kenneth Koch, James Schuyler and Barbara Guest; a second generation (Ted Berrigan, The Sonnets, 1964; Ron Padgett, Joe Brainard, Anne Waldman, Bernadette Mayer, Alice Notley) gathered around the Poetry Project at St. Mark's Church (1966).
historical_context: Abstract Expressionism and the Tibor de Nagy Gallery's editions, French Surrealism and the urban pleasures of Manhattan shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Casual, witty, improvisatory poems responsive to the present moment; the lyric, the collaborative poem and the long meditative poem (Ashbery) are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Urban detail, friendship and gossip, campy humour, surrealist leaps, painting as a model.
historical_significance: It is one of the groups in Donald Allen's The New American Poetry (1960); Ashbery's triple prize for Self-Portrait (1976) made him the most honoured poet of his generation, and the school fed into Language poetry.

name: Black Mountain Poetry
description: Poets associated with Black Mountain College in North Carolina (1933-57) and its Black Mountain Review (1954-57): Charles Olson ("Projective Verse", 1950; The Maximus Poems), Robert Creeley (For Love, 1962), Robert Duncan, Denise Levertov, Edward Dorn, Joel Oppenheimer, Jonathan Williams, Paul Blackburn and John Wieners.
historical_context: Olson's rectorship of the college (1951-56), the example of Pound and Williams, and an interest in process, field and the body shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Composition by field: the line measured by the breath, one perception leading directly to another; lyric, serial poem and long poem are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Open form, attention to syllable and line, history and place (Gloucester in Olson), anti-academic stance.
historical_significance: It is one of the groups in Donald Allen's The New American Poetry (1960) and influenced the British Poetry Revival and Language poetry.

name: Deep Image Poetry
description: American poetry built on intense, irrational images drawn from the unconscious: Robert Bly (Silence in the Snowy Fields, 1962) and his magazine The Fifties (later The Sixties), James Wright (The Branch Will Not Break, 1963), Louis Simpson, Galway Kinnell and W. S. Merwin; Jerome Rothenberg and Robert Kelly used the term "deep image" from 1960-61.
historical_context: Translations of Lorca, Neruda, Vallejo and Trakl and Jungian psychology offered an alternative to New Critical formalism; the Vietnam War gave the image political force.
aesthetic_principles: The image as a leap into the unconscious; the short free-verse lyric is the principal genre.
defining_characteristics: Silence and solitude, rural Midwestern landscape, dream imagery, anti-war protest.
historical_significance: A short-lived tendency, it shaped the 'workshop lyric' of the 1970s.

name: Concrete Poetry
description: International poetry in which the visual or sonic arrangement of letters is the poem, initiated by Eugen Gomringer and the Noigandres group of São Paulo and taken up in English by Ian Hamilton Finlay (Wild Hawthorn Press, 1961; Poor.Old.Tired.Horse., 1962-68), Edwin Morgan, dom sylvester houédard, Bob Cobbing, Mary Ellen Solt (Concrete Poetry: A World View, 1968), Emmett Williams (An Anthology of Concrete Poetry, 1967), and bpNichol and bill bissett in Canada.
historical_context: Constructivism, the Bauhaus, information theory and the new graphic design of the 1950s suggested a poetry of the material word.
aesthetic_principles: The word as object in space; visual poetry, sound poetry and the poster or inscription poem are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Spatial arrangement, minimal vocabulary, typography, permutation, the poem as sculpture or garden (Finlay's Little Sparta).
historical_significance: It peaked in the 1960s; its methods passed into visual art, sound poetry and digital poetics.

name: Language Poetry
description: American avant-garde poetry and poetics of the 1970s to 1990s that treats language itself as the medium of meaning and ideology: Charles Bernstein and Bruce Andrews (L=A=N=G=U=A=G=E, 1978-81), Barrett Watten and Robert Grenier (This, 1971), Ron Silliman (In the American Tree, 1986; The New Sentence, 1987), Lyn Hejinian (My Life, 1980), Bob Perelman, Susan Howe, Rae Armantrout and Kit Robinson, centred in the San Francisco Bay Area and New York.
historical_context: Marxist and poststructuralist theory, the legacy of Stein, Zukofsky and the New York School, and opposition to the confessional workshop lyric shaped it.
aesthetic_principles: Non-referential and disjunctive writing, the 'new sentence', the reader as co-producer of meaning; the prose poem, the serial poem and the theoretical essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Fragmentation, parataxis, critique of the lyric 'I', attention to grammar and the materiality of the signifier.
historical_significance: It succeeded the New American Poetry as the main American avant-garde and influenced British linguistically innovative poetry.

name: Performance and Spoken-Word Poetry
description: Poetry composed principally for live performance: the Last Poets (1968), Gil Scott-Heron, Jayne Cortez, the Nuyorican Poets Café (New York, 1973; Miguel Algarín, Miguel Piñero, Pedro Pietri), John Cooper Clarke in punk-era Britain, and the poetry slam begun by Marc Smith in Chicago (1984-86).
historical_context: The Black Arts Movement, the Beats and the Liverpool poets made readings central; punk, reggae and hip-hop supplied new rhythms and venues.
aesthetic_principles: Voice, rhythm and audience response as the measure of the poem; spoken word, slam, sound poetry and recorded poetry are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Political directness, humour, music and beat, identity and community, competition (the slam).
historical_significance: It overlaps with dub poetry and Black Arts poetry and prepared the spoken-word boom of the late 1990s.

name: Dub Poetry
description: Performance poetry over or in the rhythm of reggae, developed in Jamaica and Black Britain: Linton Kwesi Johnson (Dread Beat an' Blood, 1975), Oku Onuora, Michael Smith, Mutabaruka, Jean "Binta" Breeze, Benjamin Zephaniah and, in Canada, Lillian Allen.
historical_context: Reggae and the sound-system deejays, Rastafarianism, and the politics of race and policing in Jamaica and Britain in the 1970s.
aesthetic_principles: Jamaican Creole verse built on the reggae beat; recorded and performed poetry and the printed collection are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Protest against police violence and racism, history of slavery, Rastafarian vision, the rhythm of the bass line.
historical_significance: It joined Brathwaite's nation language to popular music and influenced British performance poetry and hip-hop.

name: New Formalism
description: A return to metre, rhyme and narrative in American poetry of the 1980s and 1990s: Dana Gioia ("Notes on the New Formalism", 1987; "Can Poetry Matter?", 1991), Brad Leithauser, Timothy Steele (Missing Measures, 1990), Mark Jarman and Robert McDowell (The Reaper, 1981-89), Marilyn Hacker, Molly Peacock and Rhina Espaillat; Rebel Angels: 25 Poets of the New Formalism (1996) collected them.
historical_context: Dissatisfaction with the free-verse workshop lyric and with the narrowing audience for poetry led to a revival of traditional forms, published by Story Line Press and others.
aesthetic_principles: Metrical and rhymed verse and the narrative poem; the sonnet, the villanelle, the verse narrative and the dramatic monologue are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Formal craft, accessibility, storytelling, wit.
historical_significance: It was contested by the Language poets and by critics who saw it as conservative; its debates shaped 1990s poetics.

name: The Martian Poets
description: British poets of the late 1970s and early 1980s whose poems defamiliarise everyday objects through startling metaphors: Craig Raine (A Martian Sends a Postcard Home, 1979) and Christopher Reid (Arcadia, 1979); James Fenton named the 'Martian school' in the New Statesman (1978).
historical_context: A reaction against the solemn and confessional lyric, encouraged by the editors of the New Statesman and Faber.
aesthetic_principles: The extended visual simile; the short lyric is the principal genre.
defining_characteristics: Domestic objects seen as if by an alien, playful metaphor, comic ingenuity.
historical_significance: A short-lived tendency; its metaphorical style influenced younger British poets of the 1980s.

name: Theatre of the Absurd
description: Drama that presents the human condition as meaningless through illogical action and broken dialogue; Martin Esslin named it (The Theatre of the Absurd, 1961). Its English-language writers include Samuel Beckett (Waiting for Godot, French 1953, English 1955), Harold Pinter (The Birthday Party, 1958), N. F. Simpson (A Resounding Tinkle, 1957), Edward Albee (The Zoo Story, 1959), Arthur Kopit and Tom Stoppard (Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, 1966), alongside Ionesco, Genet and Adamov in French.
historical_context: Existentialist philosophy, the aftermath of war and the nuclear threat, and the example of music hall, silent film and Surrealism.
aesthetic_principles: Circular or static action, non-sequitur, repetition and pause; the full-length play, the one-act play and the radio play are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Waiting, menace and noncommunication, tramps and clowns, bare stages, comedy turning to dread.
historical_significance: It displaced the well-made play in avant-garde theatre and coexisted with kitchen-sink realism; its methods passed into Pinter's 'comedy of menace' and later postmodern drama.

name: Kitchen-Sink Drama and the Royal Court
description: British realist drama of working-class and lower-middle-class domestic life, launched by the English Stage Company at the Royal Court Theatre under George Devine with John Osborne's Look Back in Anger (8 May 1956): Arnold Wesker (the Wesker Trilogy, 1958-60), Shelagh Delaney (A Taste of Honey, 1958, at Joan Littlewood's Theatre Workshop), John Arden (Serjeant Musgrave's Dance, 1959), Ann Jellicoe, Bernard Kops and Alun Owen; Kenneth Tynan was its critical champion.
historical_context: Post-war class mobility, the Angry Young Men and the visits of the Berliner Ensemble (1956) challenged the drawing-room comedy of the West End.
aesthetic_principles: Domestic realism and regional speech, with Brechtian and music-hall elements in Littlewood and Arden; the full-length stage play and television drama are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Bedsits and kitchens, class anger, sexual frankness, provincial and Jewish East End life.
historical_significance: It made the Royal Court the centre of new British writing and led to the political theatre of the late 1960s and the television drama of the 1960s and 1970s.

name: Political Theatre and the Fringe
description: Socialist and feminist theatre in Britain after the abolition of stage censorship by the Theatres Act 1968: Edward Bond (Saved, 1965), Howard Brenton, David Hare (Plenty, 1978), David Edgar (Destiny, 1976), Caryl Churchill (Cloud Nine, 1979; Top Girls, 1982), Trevor Griffiths (Comedians, 1975) and John McGrath, whose 7:84 Company toured The Cheviot, the Stag and the Black, Black Oil (1973); companies such as Joint Stock (1974), Monstrous Regiment (1975) and Gay Sweatshop (1975).
historical_context: The events of 1968, the end of censorship, Brecht's epic theatre and Peter Brook's Theatre of Cruelty season (1964), and new fringe venues and subsidised studios.
aesthetic_principles: Epic structure, documentary and agitprop methods, workshop devising; the full-length play, the touring show and the television play are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Class struggle and the state of Britain, feminism and sexuality, the legacy of empire, history plays about the present.
historical_significance: It moved from the fringe into the National Theatre and the Royal Shakespeare Company by the late 1970s and shaped the 'state of the nation' play.

name: Off-Off-Broadway and the American Theatre Avant-Garde
description: Experimental theatre in New York outside the commercial stage: Caffe Cino (1958), La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club (Ellen Stewart, 1961), the Judson Poets' Theater, The Living Theatre (Julian Beck and Judith Malina; The Connection, 1959), Joseph Chaikin's Open Theater (1963), Sam Shepard, María Irene Fornés, Lanford Wilson, Adrienne Kennedy (Funnyhouse of a Negro, 1964), Richard Foreman, Robert Wilson, Charles Ludlam and the Wooster Group (1975).
historical_context: Low-cost café and church venues, the counterculture, Artaud's and Grotowski's ideas and the civil-rights and anti-war movements.
aesthetic_principles: Ensemble creation, ritual, image and non-linear form; the one-act play, the performance piece and the full-length experimental play are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Physical and ritual performance, myth and pop culture, gay camp (Ludlam), dream logic, audience participation.
historical_significance: It produced the major American playwrights of the following decades and influenced performance art.

name: New Wave Science Fiction
description: Science fiction of the 1960s and early 1970s that brought literary experiment and 'inner space' into the genre: Michael Moorcock's New Worlds (from 1964), J. G. Ballard (The Atrocity Exhibition, 1970), Brian Aldiss, Thomas M. Disch, John Brunner (Stand on Zanzibar, 1968), Samuel R. Delany (Dhalgren, 1975), Roger Zelazny, Norman Spinrad, Pamela Zoline and the American writers in Harlan Ellison's Dangerous Visions (1967) and Judith Merril's England Swings SF (1968).
historical_context: The counterculture, psychoanalysis and the modernist novel, together with frustration at the technological optimism of the Campbell era.
aesthetic_principles: Psychological and stylistic experiment, sexual and political frankness; the short story, the novel and the condensed novel are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Inner space, entropy, media saturation, drugs and sexuality, dystopian satire.
historical_significance: It broke the dominance of 'hard' Golden Age SF and opened the way for feminist SF and cyberpunk.

name: Feminist Science Fiction
description: Speculative fiction that uses alternative societies and biologies to examine gender: Ursula K. Le Guin (The Left Hand of Darkness, 1969; The Dispossessed, 1974), Joanna Russ (The Female Man, 1975), James Tiptree Jr. (Alice Sheldon), Suzy McKee Charnas, Marge Piercy (Woman on the Edge of Time, 1976), Octavia E. Butler (Kindred, 1979), Sally Miller Gearhart, Joan Slonczewski and Margaret Atwood (The Handmaid's Tale, 1985).
historical_context: Second-wave feminism and the New Wave's openness to experiment; the feminist convention WisCon (1977) and the James Tiptree Jr. Award (1991) gave it institutions.
aesthetic_principles: Thought-experiment worlds that defamiliarise sex and gender; the novel and the short story are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Utopias and dystopias of gender, androgyny, reproduction and the body, race and power, critique of patriarchal SF.
historical_significance: It transformed the genre's treatment of gender and fed into the feminist literary criticism of the 1980s.

name: Cyberpunk
description: Science fiction of near-future information technology and urban decay: William Gibson ("Burning Chrome", 1982; Neuromancer, 1984), Bruce Sterling (editor of Mirrorshades, 1986), John Shirley, Rudy Rucker, Lewis Shiner, Pat Cadigan (Synners, 1991) and Neal Stephenson (Snow Crash, 1992); the term comes from Bruce Bethke's story "Cyberpunk" (1983).
historical_context: Personal computers, global networks, multinational corporations and punk culture; precursors include Philip K. Dick, Alfred Bester and the film Blade Runner (1982).
aesthetic_principles: Dense, slangy, noir-inflected prose; the novel and the short story are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Hackers and cyberspace, corporate power, body modification, street culture and the high-tech underclass.
historical_significance: It succeeded the New Wave as SF's dominant movement in the 1980s and was quickly absorbed into film and popular culture.

name: The New Criticism (Late Phase)
description: The dominant Anglo-American critical method of the 1940s and 1950s, which read the poem as an autonomous structure of tensions: Cleanth Brooks (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947), W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley ("The Intentional Fallacy", 1946; "The Affective Fallacy", 1949; The Verbal Icon, 1954), Brooks and Robert Penn Warren (Understanding Poetry, 1938), John Crowe Ransom (The New Criticism, 1941), Allen Tate, R. P. Blackmur, and René Wellek and Austin Warren (Theory of Literature, 1949).
historical_context: The expansion of American universities after the G.I. Bill made a teachable method of close reading valuable; the Kenyon Review and Sewanee Review were its journals.
aesthetic_principles: Close reading of the text itself; the critical essay, the textbook and the theoretical treatise are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Irony, paradox and ambiguity; rejection of intention, biography and reader response as criteria; organic unity.
historical_significance: It was challenged by the Chicago critics, Frye's myth criticism and, from the late 1960s, structuralism and poststructuralism, but close reading survived as the basic discipline of literary study.

name: The Chicago Critics
description: A group at the University of Chicago who proposed a pluralist, neo-Aristotelian criticism of genre and construction against the New Critics: R. S. Crane (editor of Critics and Criticism: Ancient and Modern, 1952), Elder Olson, Richard McKeon, Norman Maclean, W. R. Keast and Bernard Weinberg; Wayne C. Booth's The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961) extended the approach to narrative.
historical_context: Aristotle's Poetics and McKeon's philosophical pluralism offered an alternative to the New Critics' emphasis on irony and paradox.
aesthetic_principles: Analysis of the whole work as a constructed kind with a characteristic power; the theoretical essay and the critical treatise are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Plot, genre and the 'shaping principle', pluralism of critical frameworks, rhetoric of fiction.
historical_significance: A short-lived school whose influence survived chiefly through Booth's work on narrative rhetoric and its contribution to narratology.

name: Myth and Archetypal Criticism
description: Criticism that reads literature as a system of recurring myths, genres and archetypes: Northrop Frye (Fearful Symmetry, 1947; Anatomy of Criticism, 1957; The Secular Scripture, 1976), Leslie Fiedler ("Archetype and Signature", 1952), Philip Wheelwright and Richard Chase.
historical_context: Comparative anthropology (Frazer), Jungian psychology and the wish for a systematic, scientific criticism beyond close reading.
aesthetic_principles: Literature as an autonomous order of words organised by modes, myths and seasonal archetypes; the systematic treatise and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Romance, comedy, tragedy and irony as pre-generic narratives; displacement of myth; the 'total form' of literature.
historical_significance: Frye's Anatomy was the most cited work of criticism of its generation; structuralism took over its ambition for system.

name: Leavisite Criticism and the Scrutiny Tradition
description: The moral and evaluative criticism of F. R. Leavis and his circle: the journal Scrutiny (1932-53), The Great Tradition (1948), The Common Pursuit (1952), D. H. Lawrence: Novelist (1955), Two Cultures? The Significance of C. P. Snow (1962) and Dickens the Novelist (1970, with Q. D. Leavis), with Q. D. Leavis, L. C. Knights and Denys Thompson.
historical_context: The Cambridge English school and a belief that literary education should resist mass civilisation and the technocratic state.
aesthetic_principles: Discrimination and evaluation of 'life' in literature; the critical essay, the polemic and the evaluative monograph are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: A narrow canon of moral seriousness, hostility to Bloomsbury and to mass culture, the university as the guardian of standards.
historical_significance: It shaped English teaching in Britain and the Commonwealth and influenced the early Raymond Williams and Richard Hoggart, who turned its methods toward cultural studies.

name: Cultural Materialism and Marxist Criticism
description: Criticism that relates literature to social and economic history and ideology: in Britain Richard Hoggart (The Uses of Literacy, 1957), Raymond Williams (Culture and Society, 1958; Marxism and Literature, 1977), the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies at Birmingham (1964), Terry Eagleton (Criticism and Ideology, 1976; Literary Theory: An Introduction, 1983) and Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield (Political Shakespeare, 1985); in the United States Fredric Jameson (Marxism and Form, 1971; The Political Unconscious, 1981); the philosophers Louis Althusser and Pierre Macherey and the translated work of Lukács and Benjamin informed it.
historical_context: The New Left, adult and extra-mural education, and the translation of Western Marxist theory in the 1960s and 1970s.
aesthetic_principles: Literature read as a material practice within history and ideology; the theoretical monograph and the critical essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Class, hegemony and ideology; the 'structure of feeling' (Williams); popular culture as a serious subject.
historical_significance: It produced British cultural studies and, with New Historicism, the historicist turn of the 1980s.

name: Structuralism and Narratology
description: The analysis of literature as a system of codes and narrative structures, derived from Saussurean linguistics: Roland Barthes (Mythologies, 1957; S/Z, 1970), Gérard Genette (Narrative Discourse, 1972; English 1980), Tzvetan Todorov (who coined narratologie, 1969), A. J. Greimas, Roman Jakobson ("Linguistics and Poetics", 1960) and, in English, Jonathan Culler (Structuralist Poetics, 1975), Robert Scholes, Seymour Chatman (Story and Discourse, 1978) and Gerald Prince.
historical_context: Claude Lévi-Strauss's structural anthropology and the translation of Vladimir Propp's Morphology of the Folktale (1958); the Johns Hopkins symposium of October 1966 introduced the movement to America.
aesthetic_principles: Literature as langue rather than individual parole; the theoretical treatise and the systematic analysis are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Binary oppositions, narrative functions, focalisation, levels of narration, the death of the author.
historical_significance: It displaced New Criticism and myth criticism as the theoretical avant-garde and was itself rapidly overtaken by poststructuralism, though narratology remained a durable discipline.

name: Poststructuralism and Deconstruction
description: Theory that questions the stability of meaning, the subject and the text: Jacques Derrida ("Structure, Sign and Play", 1966; Of Grammatology, 1967, translated by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, 1976), Michel Foucault ("What Is an Author?", 1969), the late Barthes ("The Death of the Author", 1967), Julia Kristeva, and the Yale School of Paul de Man (Allegories of Reading, 1979), J. Hillis Miller, Geoffrey Hartman and Harold Bloom (Deconstruction and Criticism, 1979), with Barbara Johnson (The Critical Difference, 1980) and Jonathan Culler (On Deconstruction, 1982).
historical_context: The French philosophical critique of phenomenology and structuralism after 1968 and its rapid adoption by American English departments after the 1966 Johns Hopkins symposium.
aesthetic_principles: Close reading that exposes a text's undoing of its own oppositions; the theoretical essay and the critical monograph are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Différance and the deferral of meaning, the critique of presence and logocentrism, allegory and rhetoric, the undecidable.
historical_significance: It dominated theory in the 1970s and 1980s; the 1987 revelation of de Man's wartime collaborationist journalism and the rise of historicist and political criticism reduced its prestige.

name: Reader-Response and Reception Theory
description: Theory that locates meaning in the reader's activity or in historical reception: Hans Robert Jauss ("Literary History as a Challenge to Literary Theory", 1967) and Wolfgang Iser (The Implied Reader, 1974; The Act of Reading, 1978) of the Konstanz School; Stanley Fish (Surprised by Sin, 1967; Is There a Text in This Class?, 1980), Norman Holland, David Bleich and Louise Rosenblatt (The Reader, the Text, the Poem, 1978); Jane Tompkins's anthology Reader-Response Criticism (1980) mapped it.
historical_context: Phenomenology (Husserl, Ingarden), hermeneutics (Gadamer) and dissatisfaction with the New Critical exclusion of the reader.
aesthetic_principles: The reading process and the horizon of expectations as objects of study; the theoretical treatise and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Gaps and indeterminacy, the implied reader, interpretive communities, the history of reception.
historical_significance: It shifted attention from text to reader and influenced feminist and historicist criticism.

name: Feminist Literary Criticism
description: Criticism that examines gender in literature, the canon and the reading process: Mary Ellmann (Thinking About Women, 1968), Kate Millett (Sexual Politics, 1970), Ellen Moers (Literary Women, 1976), Elaine Showalter (A Literature of Their Own, 1977; gynocriticism), Sandra M. Gilbert and Susan Gubar (The Madwoman in the Attic, 1979), Judith Fetterley (The Resisting Reader, 1978), Barbara Smith ("Toward a Black Feminist Criticism", 1977), Annette Kolodny, bell hooks, Toril Moi (Sexual/Textual Politics, 1985) and, in French, Hélène Cixous ("The Laugh of the Medusa", 1975), Luce Irigaray and Julia Kristeva.
historical_context: The women's liberation movement and the entry of women into the academy; women's studies programmes from 1970.
aesthetic_principles: Recovery of women writers, critique of male representations of women, theory of a female literary tradition and of écriture féminine; the critical monograph, the anthology and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: The female tradition, anxiety of authorship, the resisting reader, the body and language, intersections of race, class and sexuality.
historical_significance: It reshaped the canon and the curriculum and led into gender studies and queer theory.

name: Psychoanalytic and Lacanian Criticism
description: Criticism informed by Freud and by Jacques Lacan's linguistic rereading of him: Lacan (Écrits, 1966; the seminar on "The Purloined Letter", English 1972), Harold Bloom (The Anxiety of Influence, 1973), Norman Holland, Shoshana Felman (Literature and Psychoanalysis, 1977), Juliet Mitchell (Psychoanalysis and Feminism, 1974), Peter Brooks (Reading for the Plot, 1984), Julia Kristeva (Powers of Horror, English 1982) and Slavoj Žižek (The Sublime Object of Ideology, 1989).
historical_context: The translation of Lacan and the French feminist engagement with psychoanalysis renewed a Freudian criticism that had earlier focused on authors' biographies.
aesthetic_principles: The text read for desire, repression and the structure of the subject in language; the theoretical essay and the monograph are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: The unconscious structured like a language, the mirror stage and the symbolic order, Oedipal rivalry between poets, abjection.
historical_significance: It informed feminist, film and queer theory; its claims to scientific status were attacked by critics such as Frederick Crews in the 1990s.

name: New Historicism
description: A historicist criticism that reads literary texts alongside non-literary documents as part of a culture's circulation of power: Stephen Greenblatt (Renaissance Self-Fashioning, 1980; Shakespearean Negotiations, 1988), who named it in 1982, Louis Montrose, Catherine Gallagher, Walter Benn Michaels and the journal Representations (1983); H. Aram Veeser edited The New Historicism (1989).
historical_context: Foucault's analyses of power and discourse and Clifford Geertz's 'thick description' in anthropology, together with dissatisfaction with deconstruction's apparent ahistoricism.
aesthetic_principles: The anecdote and the archive juxtaposed with the canonical text; the critical monograph and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Power, subversion and containment, self-fashioning, the textuality of history and the historicity of texts.
historical_significance: It became the leading approach in Renaissance and Romantic studies in the 1980s and is often paired with British cultural materialism.

name: Postcolonial Theory
description: Theory of colonial discourse, representation and resistance: Edward W. Said (Orientalism, 1978; Culture and Imperialism, 1993), Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (In Other Worlds, 1987; "Can the Subaltern Speak?", 1988), Homi K. Bhabha (Nation and Narration, 1990; The Location of Culture, 1994), Bill Ashcroft, Gareth Griffiths and Helen Tiffin (The Empire Writes Back, 1989), Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o (Decolonising the Mind, 1986) and Chinua Achebe ("An Image of Africa", 1975), drawing on Frantz Fanon (The Wretched of the Earth, English 1963) and the Subaltern Studies historians.
historical_context: The aftermath of decolonisation, migration to the West and poststructuralist theory of discourse.
aesthetic_principles: Analysis of representation and power, hybridity and mimicry, the subaltern voice; the theoretical monograph and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Orientalism, hybridity, the subaltern, nation and narration, the politics of language.
historical_significance: It became a major field of literary studies in the 1990s and is closely tied to postcolonial literature.

name: Queer Theory
description: Theory that questions fixed sexual and gender identities: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick (Between Men, 1985; Epistemology of the Closet, 1990), Judith Butler (Gender Trouble, 1990; Bodies That Matter, 1993), Teresa de Lauretis (who used the term 'queer theory' in 1990-91), David Halperin, Michael Warner (Fear of a Queer Planet, 1993), Diana Fuss and Leo Bersani, drawing on Michel Foucault's The History of Sexuality (volume one, English 1978).
historical_context: AIDS activism, the gay and lesbian studies of the 1980s and poststructuralist and feminist theory.
aesthetic_principles: Sexuality and gender read as discursive and performative constructions; the theoretical monograph and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Homosocial desire, the epistemology of the closet, gender performativity, anti-normativity.
historical_significance: It succeeded gay and lesbian studies as the leading theory of sexuality and influenced feminist, literary and cultural studies.

name: African American Literary Theory and the Black Aesthetic
description: Theory of Black literature from the Black Aesthetic to vernacular and Black feminist criticism: Addison Gayle Jr. (The Black Aesthetic, 1971), Larry Neal, Houston A. Baker Jr. (Blues, Ideology, and Afro-American Literature, 1984), Henry Louis Gates Jr. (The Signifying Monkey, 1988), Barbara Christian (Black Women Novelists, 1980; "The Race for Theory", 1987), Hortense Spillers, Hazel Carby (Reconstructing Womanhood, 1987), Deborah McDowell and Toni Morrison (Playing in the Dark, 1992).
historical_context: The Black Arts Movement, Black Studies programmes from 1968 and the encounter with structuralist and poststructuralist theory.
aesthetic_principles: Theory grounded in Black vernacular forms such as signifying and the blues; the theoretical monograph and the essay are the principal genres.
defining_characteristics: Signifying, the blues matrix, the Black woman's literary tradition, race as a construct in American literature.
historical_significance: It made African American literature a central field of literary theory in the 1980s and 1990s.
